The planning analysis for an AV fleet serving an AMD will require trade-offs among vehicle types, fleet configurations, and service mode operation, combined with BEV charging strategies (opportunity charging and deep charging). The transition from petroleum to electric powertrains will impact fleet operations and system cost based on vehicle operating range, charging time, charging facility location(s) and size, and availability of sufficient electric grid energy capacity. 4. ODT services will provide the base community/district circulation and FMLM service. Whether provided commercially or through a public entity (or both), ODT will form a foundational community connectivity service in future AMDs. Demand- responsive, direct origin-to-destination operations of small- to medium-sized vehicles will provide community circulation and connections to regional and interregional larger- capacity modes while enabling the optimization of energy consumption by rightsizing vehicles for passenger demand. 54 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 5. A systems engineering methodology will be needed for planning, analysis, and assessment of future AMD network systems. The SEM will essentially comprise a multisystem modeling framework, creating a “digital twin” that simulates all modes, vehicles, travelers, and critical subsystems such as charging infrastructure and vehicle dispatch. This systems engineering methodology is needed to analyze the critical parameters that determine overall system performance and bridges to a digital twin to support operations management. The SEM may also be used to investigate and integrate new forms of mobility that could augment and improve the AMD network system. At the time this report was published, initial AV functionality is in fully driverless Level 4 operation for commercial ride-hailing service in more than 10 U.S. cities, and several public mobility demonstration projects are moving forward with planned systems. As these initial systems begin to scale, NLR has identified future research needs beyond Phase III for future AMDs, summarized next. Summary of Future Research Needs Selected critical topics from Phase III research are currently being extended into the AMD Phase IV research, particularly the use of intelligent infrastructure for safety applications protecting boarding and alighting in stations/PUDO areas, as well as the continued refinement of EV integration into AV fleets with emphasis on automated charging methods and equipment. Phase IV is also beginning to explore and emphasize the following new areas of research: • AV technology advancement. Phase I began six years ago by identifying and developing a synopsis of the then 10 leading AV demonstrations/deployments. Now, more than six years later, it is necessary to revisit leading deployments and business models to bring AV technology to maturity and begin to scale. This effort will document and assess leading initiatives both in public mobility utilizing the public roadway network and for the movement of people within large facilities such as airports and medical facilities.
